name: Bench press
angleNote: Bar height: 0% = on the chest, 100% = arms locked out. Torque is per arm. Only the shoulder is analysed: see the variant notes about the elbow.

strength.note: Relative shoulder (pec / anterior deltoid) strength by bar height, assumed strongest with the bar on the chest. Indexed by bar height, not a joint angle, because the 2D view can't measure the real shoulder angle. Peak is per arm. Approximate.
strength.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

muscles.name: Pectoralis major
muscles.note: Main pressing muscle at the shoulder.

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Shoulder flexor, works with the pecs.

muscles.name: Triceps
muscles.note: Not modelled: the elbow's torque in a bench press comes from the frontal plane (bar inside or outside the elbows), which this side view can't see.

phases.name: Off the chest
phases.text: Bar on the chest, furthest in front of the shoulder: the shoulder's largest moment arm.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The bar moves back over the shoulder as it rises.

phases.name: Lockout
phases.text: Bar over the shoulder: little shoulder torque; the triceps (not modelled) finish the lift.

variants.name: Flat barbell bench press
variants.notes: Bar touches the lower chest and travels back to lock out over the shoulder. Forearms vertical, so the elbow has no torque in this view; its demand comes from the frontal plane (not modelled).

variants.name: Flat bench, bar to the upper chest
variants.notes: Touching higher keeps the bar closer over the shoulder: a smaller shoulder moment arm, but usually with more elbow flare (more shoulder stress in the frontal plane, not modelled).

variants.name: Incline bench press (30°)
variants.notes: Bench tilted 30°: the bar touches the upper chest and presses vertically over the shoulder.
